title: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (New Commissioner Functions) Bill 2019
short_title: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (New Commissioner Functions) Bill 2019

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would give the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commissioner extra regulatory powers that currently belong to the Department of Health's Secretary.
The Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission would become the single body that handles provider approvals, compliance checks, enforcement actions and compulsory assault reporting.
The changes complete a two-year reform program and are meant to reduce fragmentation in aged care regulation.
changes: The bill transfers aged care regulatory functions from the Secretary to the Commissioner.
The Commission becomes the main contact for providers and consumers on quality and regulation.
The bill streamlines how the Commissioner can impose sanctions on non-compliant providers.
The Commission takes on responsibility for compulsory assault reporting by approved providers.
The Commission approves providers for residential, home and flexible care services.
The Commission monitors provider compliance and can impose sanctions.
summary.affected: Approved providers of Australian Government funded aged care and consumers of those services.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Gee
speeches.brief: The Aged Care Legislation Amendment (New Commissioner Functions) Bill 2019 expands the powers of the independent Aged Care Quality and Safety Commissioner from 1 January 2020 to include provider approval, compliance enforcement, and administration of assault reporting, fulfilling the government's 2018-19 budget commitment and responding to the 2017 Carrell-Paterson review.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (New Commissioner Functions) Bill 2019 merely transfers existing powers from the Department of Health to the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission rather than granting new powers, and criticised the government for failing to strengthen transparency, complaints mechanisms, and arbitration. They noted 120,000 older Australians remain on a waitlist for home-care packages despite the government providing 10,000 new packages, and urged faster implementation of the royal commission’s recommendations.
